questions.question_text:
Write the equation of the line shown, and state its gradient.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}\begin{axis}[width=6cm,height=5.4cm,axis lines=middle,axis line style={-{Stealth}},xmin=-6,xmax=6,ymin=-6,ymax=6,xtick={-6,-4,-2,0,2,4,6},ytick={-6,-4,-2,0,2,4,6},grid=both,clip=false,scaled ticks=false,ticklabel style={font=\small,/pgf/number format/fixed},xlabel={$x$},ylabel={$y$}]\addplot[thick,<->,domain=-5.5:5.5,samples=2] {2};\end{axis}\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: Wrote a horizontal line as $x=$ instead of $y=$.
Gave the vertical-line gradient to a horizontal line.
Read the constant line $y=2$ as the sloped line $y=2x$.

questions.solution_text:
Every point on the line has $y$-coordinate $2$, so the equation is $y=2$.
The line is horizontal, so its gradient is $0$.

questions.question_text:
Write the equation of the line that is parallel to the $x$-axis and passes through the point shown.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}\begin{axis}[width=6cm,height=5.4cm,axis lines=middle,axis line style={-{Stealth}},xmin=-6,xmax=6,ymin=-6,ymax=6,xtick={-6,-4,-2,0,2,4,6},ytick={-6,-4,-2,0,2,4,6},grid=both,clip=false,scaled ticks=false,ticklabel style={font=\small,/pgf/number format/fixed},xlabel={$x$},ylabel={$y$}]\addplot[only marks,mark=*,mark size=2pt] coordinates {(5,-1)};\node[above left] at (axis cs:5,-1) {$(5,-1)$};\end{axis}\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: Used the x-coordinate; a line parallel to the x-axis uses the y-value.
Used the x-coordinate as the constant instead of the y-coordinate.
Used the y-value but wrote it as a vertical $x=$ equation.

questions.solution_text:
A line parallel to the $x$-axis is horizontal, so it uses the point's $y$-coordinate.
The point has $y$-coordinate $-1$, so the equation is $y=-1$.

questions.question_text:
A line passes through the points $(2,-4)$ and $(2,1)$. Write its equation and state its gradient.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}\begin{axis}[width=6cm,height=5.4cm,axis lines=middle,axis line style={-{Stealth}},xmin=-6,xmax=6,ymin=-6,ymax=6,xtick={-6,-4,-2,0,2,4,6},ytick={-6,-4,-2,0,2,4,6},grid=both,clip=false,scaled ticks=false,ticklabel style={font=\small,/pgf/number format/fixed},xlabel={$x$},ylabel={$y$}]\addplot[only marks,mark=*,mark size=2pt] coordinates {(2,-4) (2,1)};\node[right] at (axis cs:2,-4) {$(2,-4)$};\node[right] at (axis cs:2,1) {$(2,1)$};\end{axis}\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]

options.why: Wrote the shared x-value as a horizontal $y=$ equation.
Gave a vertical line the horizontal gradient of $0$.
Used a single y-coordinate rather than the shared x-value.

questions.solution_text:
Both points have the same $x$-coordinate $2$, so the line is vertical.
Every point has $x$-coordinate $2$, so the equation is $x=2$.
A vertical line has an undefined gradient.
